articles.title: The government has delayed the toughest spending decisions – but here’s what we do know after the budget
articles.author: Steve Schifferes, Honorary Research Fellow, City Political Economy Research Centre, City St George's, University of London
paras: John Healey’s steady-as-she-goes budget was a picture of a government doing its best to offer “what help we can afford”, while weathering the economic storms. But despite its 98 policy measures, decisions on some of the biggest issues appear to have been kicked down the road.

In the meantime, it seems that the real incomes of UK households could fall by 1% next year. This forecast, from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), offered a grim picture. It also predicted UK economic growth of just 1%, as well as higher inflation and interest rates. The OBR, the government’s independent spending watchdog, has also suggested that by 2029-30 households will still be only 1% better off than they were ten years previously. This would be the slowest growth in real disposable household income for generations.

And in further bad news for households, the OBR estimated that the tax collected by the government as a percentage of GDP would reach record levels by 2030-31 – six percentage points higher than pre-pandemic levels. Taxes are already higher than at any time since the second world war.

The budget was enthusiastically backed by Labour members. But it can also be seen as a holding operation by the chancellor, reassuring the markets while leaving the prime minister the space to develop his vision of the causes close to his heart. These of course include social care, devolution and welfare reform. Notably, the only measure which in relative terms was generously funded was the £500 million allocated to end rough sleeping, the cause Burnham cited as his priority on his first day in office.
The limited measures to help with the cost of living reflect Burnham’s concerns about tackling the issue that most worries the public, but they are modest in scale and for the most part temporary.

The Treasury’s modest ambitions are reflected in the limited scale of the additional taxes it has announced to fund cost-of-living measures, especially to help with energy prices. The government has found some taxes it can raise and some efficiency savings it could make.

However, most of the cost-of-living measures – which will cost £6.5 billion this year – are only temporary, while some of the tax increases occur later in the parliament. As a result, the government expects that within five years the situation will be reversed, with Treasury revenues up by £7 billion.

One move that could have a long-term impact is Healey’s changes to the spending rules to protect “preventive spending” from department cuts. These are measures that have an initial cost but eventually save money. An example is the SureStart childcare programme, for example, which has been shown to improve long-term education prospects and reduce crime in deprived communities.
Back to welfare and defence

But the government has postponed its most difficult decisions – on defence, social care, devolution and welfare spending. The latter, the most politically challenging, awaits the publication of two key reports on welfare next month. The Timms and Milburn reviews will report respectively on personal independence payments, and the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).

Any big decisions are likely to take shape after the publication of the prime minister’s ten-year plan (expected in December), and next year’s spending review, which will flesh out spending plans up to the next general election.

The urgent need to boost defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030 was the issue that led Healey to resign from the previous government. In his first budget as chancellor, despite insisting this target would be met, he was cagey on how it might be financed.

He cited “innovative financing measures”, which might include off-the-books contributions from the private sector through PFI (private finance initiatives) and the use of government investment banks, which may not be subject to the same fiscal rules. Healey also sees defence spending as part of the government’s industrial strategy, and ministers have announced that foreign firms that win defence contracts of more than £50 million will have to deliver benefits of the same amount back into the UK.

Another thing we do know is that defence investment will also be funded by forcing all other departments to cut their own spending by 1%. This is a pattern Healey may repeat to fund other new spending commitments.

In fact, the OBR estimates that, after taking into account the future spending plans of the “protected” departments (health, education and defence), all other departments would need to cut their own spending by 2.6% to allow the government to meet its 2030-31 fiscal target. This would mean less for roads, prisons, the police, housing, and higher education. “Efficiency savings” would be unlikely to close the gap.

The chancellor has taken over at a particularly difficult time for the world economy, and European nations are among the hardest hit. Healey will need luck as well as skill to navigate the shoals of a global slowdown. However, it is already clear that the prime minister’s desire for closer ties with Europe to boost growth is not shared by the chancellor.

Many events – from a resumption of full-scale warfare in the Strait of Hormuz to the possible collapse of the AI bubble – are beyond Healey’s control. He has temporarily reassured the bond markets with his cautious “do no harm” budget. But delivering improved living standards and better public services to a still-jaundiced electorate remains an enduring challenge.

articles.title: Massive sinkholes open up across Turkey as it struggles with drought and climate change
articles.author: Nima Shokri, Adjunct Professor, Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH), United Nations University; Technical University of Hamburg
paras: Turkey’s central Anatolian plateau is one of the country’s most important agricultural regions, producing wheat, maize, sugar beet and other crops. Yet beneath its cultivated fields, the ground is becoming increasingly unstable.
Large sinkholes, some tens of metres wide and deep, have appeared across the Konya basin, swallowing farmland, and threatening nearby roads and settlements.
These collapses can occur suddenly, sometimes in fields that have been cultivated for generations. Around 20 are opening up every year, according to a recent study.
Known locally as obruks, sinkholes are not a new geological phenomenon. They have existed in the Konya basin for thousands of years, but they have become far more frequent over recent decades.

Konya’s sinkholes are consequently both a geological hazard and evidence of a wider water-management problem. The cavities beneath the fields are the product of geological processes extending over thousands of years. Their recent instability, however, is occurring within a groundwater system profoundly altered by human activity and increasingly exposed to drought.

As representatives of countries all over the world prepare to head to Turkey to discuss climate change at the UN’s Cop 31 conference, Ankara continues to grapple with this escalating environmental disaster at home.
The nation’s disaster and emergency management authority (AFAD) has recently documented 684 sinkholes across Konya, Karaman and Aksaray in Turkey’s agricultural heartlands.
The growing number of sinkholes is often attributed to drought and climate change. But intensive groundwater extraction for agriculture can also increase the risk of collapse.

Decades of intensive agricultural irrigation have altered the conditions beneath the basin’s surface. Groundwater, which is the layer of water below the Earth’s surface, is also not being replenished during long, dry periods, which adds to the problem.

Konya is a closed drainage basin. This means water entering the basin does not flow towards the sea. It is stored underground, and accumulates in lakes and wetlands, or returns to the atmosphere through evaporation and plant transpiration.

Rainfall is relatively low here, and much of it falls outside the main growing season. Groundwater has, therefore, become indispensable to agriculture, particularly for irrigated maize, sugar beet and fodder crops.

The difficulty is that demand for water has grown beyond the rate at which the aquifers, a body of porous rock or sediment saturated with groundwater, can recover. A recent regional study estimated an average annual loss of groundwater storage, equivalent to 3.4 centimetres of water. This figure clearly points to a system under sustained pressure.
Part of the problem is that Turkey experienced its most severe drought for decades in 2025, putting more pressure on farmers.

Farmers often respond by extracting more groundwater, causing underground water levels to fall. This reduces the pressure exerted by water within the pores and fractures of rocks and sediments, potentially destabilising existing underground cavities and increasing the risk of collapse.

The consequences extend beyond water scarcity, because groundwater also puts stress on underground geological formations. The Konya basin contains extensive carbonate rocks, including limestone. Over long periods, groundwater circulating through fractures dissolves minerals and enlarges openings. This process, known as karstification, can produce underground channels, caves and cavities. Sinkholes form when the material above such voids becomes unstable.

Lower groundwater levels can also change the movement of water and sediment through existing underground cavities, allowing loose material to shift downwards. Where the roof of a cavity is already weak, these changes may eventually lead to collapse.

But the response is highly dependent on local conditions. The depth and shape of underground cavities, the thickness and strength of the layers of rock and sediment above them, the distribution of fractures and the history of groundwater fluctuations all matter.

This helps explain an important finding from a study on sinkhole formation in the Konya basin between 2000 and 2024. The researchers identified a sharp increase in the annual formation rate, from approximately three sinkholes a year during 2000-10 to 32 during 2016-19. Yet the rate subsequently declined to around 22 a year after 2020, despite continuing groundwater depletion.

If falling groundwater is responsible, why would fewer sinkholes form while water levels continue to decline? One possible explanation is that the most vulnerable cavities in some areas have already collapsed. Sinkhole formation depends on the number of unstable underground structures, not simply on the volume of water extracted.

The basin is also experiencing another type of ground deformation, known as land subsidence, in which the surface gradually sinks as underground sediments compact. This can cause cracks in the ground and damage to roads and buildings, although the sinking is often too gradual to notice without satellite measurements.

Satellite radar measurements revealed widespread land subsidence in the area, of up to 90 millimetres per year. Unlike sudden sinkhole collapse, this can develop as groundwater withdrawal increases stress on the land and compresses sediments in the ground.

The problem is not unique to Turkey. A global analysis estimated that over 6.3 million square kilometres of land are subsiding by more than five millimetres annually. The researchers identified groundwater extraction as the most influential factor worldwide.

In Konya, the pressure on groundwater is closely connected to agricultural production. Farmers cultivate crops for established markets and processing industries, often under policies that have favoured high levels of production, rather than water conservation.
Irrigation provides a way for farmers to maintain yields of crops during dry years, but it also allows production to continue at levels that the basin’s renewable water supply may not sustain.

However, restricting how much groundwater is extracted without providing support for farmers could impose substantial economic pressure on them, as well as on the nation’s food supply. But continued groundwater depletion could progressively undermine the agricultural production that made the region economically important in the first place.

More efficient irrigation could help, but is not enough. If water saved through improved technology is used to expand the area being irrigated, total groundwater consumption may remain unchanged or even increase.

A long-term response would require reliable monitoring of groundwater levels and withdrawals, enforceable extraction limits, agricultural incentives aligned with local water availability and detailed mapping of geological hazards. Satellite measurements can help identify areas under pressure.
The most immediate danger is that another field, road or building may collapse, putting lives at risk.

Preventing the next sinkhole is difficult. The government could address the problem. But it needs to introduce agricultural policies that treat groundwater as a finite resource, rather than a permanent substitute for rainfall.
Nima Shokri is affiliated with Hamburg University of Technology.

articles.title: How different election results affect bank stability – global study
articles.author: George Kladakis, Lecturer in Finance, University of St Andrews
paras: Recent elections in Brazil and Israel have yielded different political outcomes. In Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s narrow and ultimately surprise victory in a presidential runoff vote has kept him in office.

In Israel, meanwhile, an inconclusive election result has left uncertainty over the formation of the next government. These outcomes are likely to have an effect on the stability of the financial systems in both countries.

Historically, financial experts believed elections primarily caused brief, nervous jitters in national stock markets. As prior evidence shows, the impact of political uncertainty is often concentrated around the election period, with short-lived spikes in market volatility.
But our 2026 study of 147 national elections across 22 OECD economies between 2000 and 2023 reveals a much deeper, longer-lasting reality.

To understand this, we must first demystify a common banking term: systemic risk. This is the financial equivalent of a domino effect. It is the danger that a shock to one institution or sector could trigger a widespread collapse across the entire financial system.

We saw this in action on a large scale during the 2008 global financial crisis. At that time, the distress of a few highly interconnected institutions threatened to bring down the entire global financial system. Massive government intervention was required to stop the dominoes from falling.

Our findings show that systemic risk follows a broadly hump-shaped trajectory. It dips before scheduled elections, then rises during and after the vote. The risk remains elevated for up to 12 months, particularly when the incumbent government loses office.

Pre-election spending that supports economic activity, alongside possible government suppression of adverse information about economic and financial conditions, offers an explanation for the temporary calm observed before elections.
How elections affect systemic risk

Our study suggests that political continuity can be a financial asset for national banking systems. But Brazil’s recent experience nevertheless shows that continuity does not automatically reassure investors.

Lula reversed a first-round election deficit of more than 2 million votes to secure his reelection. This was the first time since Brazil’s 1985 return to democracy that a president has managed to overturn a first-round defeat.
So the result surprised markets that had positioned for Lula’s challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, to take office.

On October 26, the day after the runoff vote, Brazil’s benchmark stock index fell 13.9%, while its currency lost 8.1% against the US dollar. There was a modest recovery the following day, with stocks gaining around 1%.

The immediate market reaction does not suggest a banking crisis is underway in Brazil. Whether it develops into broader financial instability depends on how financial institutions and borrowers absorb the shock.

Our study also found that elections that yield no clear winner raise systemic risk, as they leave policy uncertainty over budgets and regulation unresolved. Israel has long struggled to establish durable governing coalitions, and its October 27 election left neither main bloc with a parliamentary majority.

While the US president, Donald Trump, had openly endorsed Israel’s incumbent prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, some investors had been positioning for a change of government. The inconclusive result has unsettled markets that had anticipated a clearer political outcome.

During trading on October 28, the day after the election, Israeli stocks fell around 3%. Israel’s currency, the shekel, also weakened by approximately 2% against the US dollar. And the ten-year government bond yield rose nearly five basis points to 4.13%, signalling higher borrowing costs.

Finally, our data shows that snap elections are associated with larger increases in systemic risk. Here, again, Israel is an instructive example. Israel experienced ten elections between 2000 and 2023, seven of which were snap elections. This included five snap elections during its 2018-22 political crisis.
Strong economic growth and high public trust in government cushion the financial blow of elections, as they naturally insulate the banking system.

Macroprudential policies, the regulatory guardrails designed to protect the entire banking system, also play a crucial role. By strengthening financial safeguards such as capital buffers for banks, regulators can help the system absorb political shocks.

Unfortunately, evidence suggests that political incentives to stimulate lending before an election can encourage the loosening of these safeguards. This leaves national financial systems more exposed to subsequent shocks.
In Turkey and India, for example, governments have historically used state-owned banks to expand consumer and mortgage credit aggressively before tightly contested elections.

This creates a short-term boost in economic activity and voter goodwill, but often leaves the financial system vulnerable to a hangover of non-performing loans and instability once the votes are counted.

As well as being political events, elections are macroeconomic shockwaves. While the stock market might experience a brief spike in volatility on election night, the true test lies in the systemic risk that lingers in the banking sector for months afterwards.

In Brazil, Lula eventually secured backing from voters for a fourth presidential term. Strengthening financial stability there after this surprise result will require rebuilding market confidence with a credible fiscal plan that explains how campaign promises will be funded and puts public debt on a sustainable path.

In Israel, prospects for a viable government remain uncertain. And even if one emerges, it may offer markets only limited reassurance while the war in the Middle East continues to pose risks to financial stability in Israel and worldwide.

articles.title: Faculty and students show how reporting is done when a university partners with local news
articles.author: Teri Finneman, Professor of Journalism, University of Kansas
paras: Catherine Bilskie, the advertising and office manager for the newspaper in Solon, Iowa, had seen many local news outlets close. So she was sure her job at the Solon Economist was about to go one Friday morning in February 2024.

But to her surprise, a new owner, Jason Brummond, appeared. He not only promised to keep her and her co-worker employed at the weekly paper but assured them raises if they agreed to an unusual new venture. And he wasn’t a wealthy benefactor or a representative from a private equity firm – he came from the University of Iowa.

It’s just one example of academic institutions stepping up to address the “news desert” crisis: Thousands of communities across the U.S. have lost local newspapers over the past two decades. And journalism faculty, staff and students are increasingly working together to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications for communities lacking local news outlets.

These partnerships have ranged from the Spanish-language news site Noticiero Móvil at the University of Nevada, Reno, to “Good Morning Indian Country” at the University of Kansas, to The Scope at Northeastern in Boston.

We’re journalism professors who have studied and experienced the opportunities and challenges of running community news through higher education. Our new book, “News Desert U,” asks whether this approach is one solution to saving local news. We believe the need is urgent given the stakes and the scope of the crisis.
These experiments come against a grim backdrop.

Over 3,000 newspapers have closed in the U.S. in the past 20 years, including about 170 in 2025, according to Northwestern’s 2026 State of Local News report. Causes include an antiquated business model, declining advertising revenue and hedge-fund buyouts that have gutted papers. Northwestern’s 2025 report estimated that total print newspaper circulation has declined 70% in the past 20 years.
But university partnerships can show promise, we found, with the help of the next generation of journalists.

Iowa’s Solon Economist is one example. The University of Iowa doesn’t actually own the paper, or its sister paper, the Mount Vernon-Lisbon Sun. Still, the relationship is key to making the new venture work.

Its owner, Brummond, is also the publisher of the University of Iowa’s student newspaper, the Daily Iowan, which is owned and operated by the nonprofit Student Publications. While the student newspaper office is inside the journalism school’s building, it operates independently.

In August 2023, Student Publications began talks about buying the Sun and the Economist after the weeklies’ then owner reached out about selling the publications. With both newspapers 20-30 minutes from campus, discussions included how the faculty and students could help the papers.

The Journalism School’s director, Melissa Tully, was immediately in favor – provided that the newspapers’ existing professional staff stay and not be replaced with students. In addition to the editors, this included keeping the advertising and circulation staff.

“They know these communities. So that was really important just from a moral and ethical imperative, but also from a news perspective,” she said. “They’re trusted in their communities. They know what’s going on.”

Student Publications bought both newspapers for US$10,000 in 2024. Since then, circulation has remained stable at both, Brummond said, even as many other publications across the country have suffered declines.
Meanwhile, students in classes such as community news, high school sports, social media marketing and photography contribute for academic credit while other students do paid internships.
Solon Economist Editor Chris Umscheid said he welcomes a revolving door of student interns because it means he’s “actually going to have staff for once.”
“People thought we were going to be the university’s paper, and we’re not,” he said. “I don’t anticipate anything changing there. We’re still going to focus on everything Solon that we can.”

The success has led to Student Publications getting requests to buy other newspapers, Tully said, and it’s working on a list of criteria to consider future partnerships. Brummond cautions these arrangements aren’t easy to pull off, as they require a careful review of finances, workflow and logistical complications that come with a merger.
Liz King, who served as Solon Public Library director, said many locals were afraid the newspaper would close, which would have been a hard blow for the town of about 3,000.
Some readers only get their news through the newspaper, she said. “They’re not comfortable with online sources.”
Dink NeSmith had a similar close scare in Georgia with the The Oglethorpe Echo.

Owner Ralph Maxwell had decided in September 2021 that he had no choice but to shutter the paper due to his own health issues, revenue declines and lack of interest from prospective buyers. He gave NeSmith, an old friend and retired newspaper owner, an early heads-up.
“I don’t know that I want to live in a town that doesn’t have its newspaper,” was NeSmith’s response. He told Maxwell: “You can’t close the Echo.”
NeSmith immediately reached out to the University of Georgia’s journalism school to suggest a partnership.

In the meantime, NeSmith worked to set up a separate nonprofit, Oglethorpe Echo Legacy, for the paper’s new ownership structure. Keeping the newspaper’s finances independent of the university was an important step to ensure the paper would not be subject to any possible “whims” of future administrations, as Charles Davis, the journalism school’s dean, put it. That status was also a signal to Oglethorpe County that the paper’s goal was to serve the community, not make money, he added.
The new nonprofit bought the paper from Maxwell in October 2021 for $10 – a check that Maxwell never cashed and has since been framed.

Davis asked Andy Johnston, an adjunct professor with decades of journalism experience, to serve as the newspaper’s full-time editor. Since November 2021, Johnston has led a team of journalism faculty and students, with the help of several adult staff and volunteers from the county.

The paper covers a wide terrain. Oglethorpe County has over 16,000 people stretching over 442 square miles, and Lexington, where the Echo has its office, is 18 miles (29 kilometers) from the campus in Athens. The reporting staff is provided by journalism professor Amanda Bright’s capstone class – 20 students each semester. Supplementary funding comes from the journalism school, various grants and Echo subscription and advertising funds.

She pairs two students to each beat, with one in charge of a story and the other in charge of editing and producing, with a rotation each week. Students need to turn in eight stories a semester – with corresponding editing and producing assignments that include video, an email newsletter and social media – to get class credit.

When the journalism school took over, the weekly had only a printed newspaper, with no website, social media presence or other digital products, she said. So in their first print edition, the editors outlined their plan for the newspaper to readers and then introduced the student reporters, which they still do every semester.

The partnership has paid off. Print subscriptions to The Echo have doubled and overall digital audience has quadrupled thanks to the launch of new digital products, Bright said. Advertising revenue, meanwhile, has tripled, she said. However, it took some time for local businesses to get used to advertising again, NeSmith said.

But many challenges remain. Johnston has to handle student turnover every semester while students covering events such as government meetings face a steep learning curve and need support. The additional time it takes to edit student copy means content doesn’t appear as quickly. Many faculty members have to work long hours to keep the paper afloat.
But the broader impact is clear: More than two dozen students have gone into local news as a career following their time at the Echo, Bright said.

Should other universities want to follow this model, they need at least two key people in leadership, whether that’s two faculty members or one from faculty and a professional editor, Bright said. “That’s a bottom-line necessity for sanity,” she added.
One common theme from our research is that a service-oriented approach to news that addresses the community’s needs takes priority over profit at these partnerships.

The built-in advantages for these initiatives is that the faculty and staff who tend to manage them get their paychecks and health insurance from their university work. They don’t need to draw a living wage from the news outlet’s finances.

These partnerships are also ideal for students seeking real-world experience while earning class credit or internship wages. And journalism schools are already stocked with multimedia equipment that students can use for their reporting.

Still, they can look deceptively simple on the surface, Brummond said. Tully, at the University of Iowa, recommends other interested universities should go slowly. Building a successful project takes patient experimentation and a willingness to regroup when needed, in her view.
“Doing this slowly is OK,” she said. “In the end, it’s going to be better. So far, that’s been a good recipe for us.”
Teri Finneman and Pamela Walck are co-authors of the book "News Desert U."

Pamela E. Walck does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: How the law protecting Americans from surprise medical bills is driving up healthcare costs
articles.author: Lindsey Murtagh, Distinguished Senior Fellow in Health Law, Brown University
paras: Imagine you get hit by a car. An ambulance brings you to the nearest hospital. Your private health insurance covers emergency care, but the hospital isn’t in your plan’s network.
Before 2022, if you received emergency care from an out-of-network provider or hospital, you could get hit with an extra, often huge bill on top of what you owe as a copay, coinsurance or deductible.

A law called the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022, was designed to protect people with private health insurance from just these situations. It limits your costs to what you would have paid if the ambulance had brought you to an in-network hospital or you were treated by an in-network provider instead.

As a health policy researcher and a former federal employee who helped draft the rules to implement the No Surprises Act, I applaud the law’s success in preventing patients from being hit with surprise medical bills in most cases.

However, a small number of out-of-network providers are using the law to extract enormous payments from health plans. This behavior is starting to drive up the cost of coverage for both employers and individuals. In my view, if left unaddressed, these increases will only get steeper.

The No Surprises Act was designed to address a troublesome feature of the U.S. healthcare system: It is notoriously difficult to predict how much your healthcare will cost. This is especially true when someone receives out-of-network care.

Before the law went into effect, roughly 20% of inpatient emergency department visits resulted in a surprise bill from an out-of-network provider. Surprise bills are common for other types of care too. One study found roughly 40% of air ambulance rides resulted in a surprise bill, costing an average of almost US$20,000.

The threat of these bills exacted an enormous emotional and financial toll. Roughly two-thirds of Americans reported being very or somewhat worried about unexpected medical bills, according to a 2020 poll conducted by KFF, a national health policy nonprofit.

The No Surprises Act protects Americans from certain instances of a practice called balance billing, in which an out-of-network hospital or doctor asks you to pay the difference between what they billed for a service and what your insurance agreed to pay for it.

When a provider joins your plan’s network, they agree to accept a specific payment for a given service or procedure. They agree to charge you only for cost sharing, such as a copayment, coinsurance or deductible, and they aren’t allowed to balance bill you.

However, plans can’t prevent out-of-network providers or facilities from balance billing. On top of that, your own plan may also charge you a higher copayment, coinsurance or deductible when you go out of network. That’s why out-of-network care can be much more expensive than in-network care.

The No Surprises Act protects consumers from these extra costs in cases where they have little or no control over whether they see an in- or out-of-network doctor. The law prohibits balance billing and requires cost sharing to be at approximately in-network levels in three cases where surprise medical bills were common:

If you receive out-of-network emergency care at a hospital or independent freestanding emergency facility. In a medical emergency, you’re not expected to figure out whether the closest hospital is in-network. You can’t be balance billed.

If an out-of-network provider treats you during a visit to an in-network hospital or ambulatory surgical center. For example, if an out-of-network anesthesiologist cares for you during a surgery at an in-network hospital, that anesthesiologist cannot balance bill you.
If you receive out-of-network air ambulance services.

The No Surprises Act doesn’t prevent big, unexpected medical bills in all cases. For example, you can still get balance billed for ground ambulance services or if you see an out-of-network doctor outside of a hospital or ambulatory surgical center.

The No Surprises Act is working as promised for patients – as of September 2026, it has prevented approximately 50 million surprise medical bills. But there’s a downside: Employers and unions are raising the alarm that the No Surprises Act is increasing the cost of providing health insurance.
What’s driving up costs is an arbitration process run amok.

Rather than specifying how much insurance plans should pay out-of-network providers, the law allows providers who are dissatisfied with the plan’s payment to bring disputes to arbitration. Each side submits an offer. The arbitrator must select one party’s offer as the out-of-network payment.

To choose an offer, the arbitrator considers information submitted by both parties. Information can vary by case. But the law requires the arbitrator to always consider an amount that is basically the middle amount the health plan pays in-network providers for the same service.

Health policy experts like me anticipated most disputes would be settled close to this amount. Over time, experts expected this would put downward pressure on the cost of healthcare and result in payments to both in- and out-of-network providers going down. The Congressional Budget Office predicted these lower payments would reduce premiums for consumers by 1% and reduce federal deficits by $17 billion.

As a federal employee, I worked on rules that would have required the arbitrators to treat the middle amount as a strong benchmark. I expected those rules to achieve savings like those predicted by the Congressional Budget Office. But lawsuits from providers blocked those rules from going into effect.
Without those rules, arbitrators are selecting offers that are far above what plans would pay in-network. The winning offers are also much larger than what Medicare would pay for the same service.

Providers are winning the vast majority – roughly 85% – of these disputes. They are also using arbitration more than expected. The federal government estimated there would be 17,000 disputes annually. Last year, there were more than 2 million disputes, many brought by providers with private equity investment. And the volume of disputes has grown every year.
Frequent and big provider wins at arbitration will not put downward pressure on healthcare prices. They will likely do the opposite.
When a provider wins an arbitration dispute, an individual patient’s cost sharing doesn’t change. It is capped at what the in-network amount would have been.

However, consumers as a group are the ones who ultimately will pay for the cost of arbitration. Researchers estimate the arbitration process alone cost health plans $22.4 billion in the law’s first four years. This doesn’t include the increases in in-network rates that are likely to occur if arbitration trends continue on pace.
I’m concerned that to pay for this, insurance companies will increase rates. Employers will need to budget more to pay for health insurance or increase the amount their employees pay.

We’re already seeing the costs of arbitration affect the price of health insurance. The New York state employee plan reported that the No Surprises Act was a key driver behind the plan’s 10% rate hike for 2027. A Texas city reported the No Surprises Act caused its employee plan to exceed its 2026 budget by $40 million.

Right now, only a small portion of providers use arbitration. If volume continues to grow and providers continue to win big, the cost of arbitration will grow as well – and so too will costs for consumers.
With healthcare costs a huge concern for Americans and a major issue in the 2026 midterm elections, the No Surprises Act is under scrutiny.

Congress appears interested in addressing this threat to affordability. In September 2026, the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee hosted a roundtable to discuss options to fix the law. In October, U.S. Rep. Frank Pallone, a New Jersey Democrat, introduced legislation to scuttle the arbitration system entirely.
Absent action by Congress, I fear that the protection the No Surprises Act offers Americans will come at a cost that ultimately limits consumers’ access to health insurance.
Lindsey Murtagh receives funding from Arnold Ventures

articles.title: 70 years ago the Suez crisis exposed British relative decline. Today, the Iran conflict could be doing the same for the US
articles.author: Eoin McLaughlin, Professor in Economics, University College Cork
paras: Months after the US and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran, the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed. The UK chose not to get directly involved in the conflict. Nonetheless, it has been exposed to the crisis through record-high diesel prices as well as a spike in inflation.
This echoes an earlier crisis in the Middle East, as my recent research illustrates.

Seventy years ago, the Egyptian government nationalised the Suez canal, sparking the Suez crisis. The canal, which passes through Egypt from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, was a vital link for ships travelling between Europe and Asia.

After its completion in 1869 by a French-led company, the Egyptian government held a 44% stake in it. However, financial difficulties forced Egypt to sell its shares to the British government in 1875, leaving Britain and France with substantial financial interests in the canal.

Following the Egyptian nationalisation of the canal, France and Britain – together with Israel – invaded Egypt in an attempt to regain control of the vital waterway. But the invasion was a spectacular failure that was condemned by the international community. The crisis came to symbolise Britain’s loss of superpower status.

Today, the US midterm elections are increasing the pressure on the Trump administration over the current conflict. Elections in Israel have also had some bearing on the conflict, with recent reports that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushed for renewed strikes ahead of the election. Other reports suggest that the US and Israel have drawn up plans to resume strikes after the elections.

In 1956, US presidential elections were also an important part of the calculus. But back then, Britain and France had assumed that the elections would distract the US from their actions. This was a miscalculation. In communication with UK Prime Minister Anthony Eden the day after the vote, US President Dwight D. Eisenhower was clear that his administration would not tolerate the UK, France and Israel’s continued actions. He demanded a negotiated settlement through the UN.
The parallels between Suez and Hormuz go beyond the closure of two vital waterways. Both crises raise the same question: how far can geopolitical power outrun economic power?

In 1944, the American foreign policy professor William T.R. Fox coined the term “super-power”. He defined it as the consequence of “great wealth, great population, and favourable geographic position”. This is similar to how the historian Phillips O’Brien defines great power today. Fox saw three superpowers at that time: the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union. He later acknowledged that including Britain had been a mistake, primarily because of its relative decline against the US and later the rest of Europe.
Arguably a similar shift is taking place today.

There are arguments over what is the best measure of an economy, but on the basis of purchasing power the shift is striking. China has moved from being a fraction of the size of the US economy in 1990 to being well ahead today.

In the 19th century, Britain was the dominant global power and benefited from what economists call “exorbitant privilege”. This was the ability to easily finance debt at favourable interest rates because sterling played a central role in the international monetary system. London was also the world’s leading financial centre.

But as Britain declined, this privilege gradually shifted towards the US. Its loss became particularly pressing during the Suez crisis as the pound came under intense pressure. Similarly today, there are signs of strain in the financial system that underpins American power.
During the Suez crisis, Britain’s currency weakness and dependence on American financial support constrained its ability to act independently, despite its considerable military power.

The crisis was also part of wider cold war geopolitics. An arms deal signed in 1955 between Egypt and the Soviet Union had upset the regional balance of power and contributed to Israel’s decision to get involved in a preventative war.

In response to the arms deal, the US withdrew financing for the Aswan Dam, a major infrastructure project on the River Nile. Then, in 1956, Egypt nationalised the Suez canal, sparking the crisis. British leaders sought to portray Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser as a 1930s dictator, intent on regional dominance.

The US intervention in Iran has similar connotations. US secretary of war Pete Hegseth has presented the assassination of the Iranian leadership as necessary to prevent an existential threat from “America’s mortal enemy”.

Geoeconomics, the relationship between economics and geopolitics, also played a central role in the Suez crisis. The canal was a major conduit for Middle Eastern oil and there were fears that the nationalisation of the canal would disrupt UK oil supplies. But ironically, it was the decision to invade Egypt that led to a shortage of oil and fuel rationing in the UK.

The wider cold war was a key factor in the US stance on events. The US did not want to be seen to be condoning imperial actions in Egypt while condemning Russian imperialism in Hungary. Just as the Suez crisis needs to be understood in the context of the cold war, the current conflict should also be seen through the lens of “cold war II” geopolitics. Relations between the US and China have not thawed, while proxy wars bear similarities to the first cold war.

Today, the US is increasingly stretched, most clearly seen in the depletion of its munitions. These were already under pressure (in part because of its support for Ukraine) and have been further reduced by the war with Iran.

The Suez crisis illustrates how political leaders can be slow to appreciate the economic constraints on their geopolitical ambitions. The US today is not Britain in 1956, yet the conflict in Iran has prompted questions about the limits of American power. As its relative economic dominance is challenged, will the US also have to reconsider the extent of its global military commitments?

Eoin McLaughlin does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: 1 in 4 Pennsylvanians say they paid out of pocket for their annual checkup. Why isn’t insurance covering these preventive visits?
articles.author: Sujeong Park, Assistant Professor of Health Policy and Addiction Studies, Penn State
paras: I was teaching health economics when a student raised his hand. We were discussing the Affordable Care Act, or ACA, which requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services at no additional cost to patients. I explained that preventive care could cost nothing.

The student had expected that, too. Instead, he said, he received a bill for more than US$500 after his checkup. He was so frustrated that he said he would never go back for another annual checkup. I suggested he contact his insurer to find out why he had been charged and whether his visit had been billed as preventive care.
Then another student spoke up. Her husband had paid several hundred dollars for what he thought would be a free checkup too.

The very next day, I received a $78 bill for my own Pap smear. I expected my insurance to cover this cervical cancer screening without cost-sharing because it is among the preventive services recommended by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force and generally covered under the ACA.

When I called my insurer, I learned that the visit had been billed as a regular outpatient office visit, with no mention of the Pap smear. I then called my primary care provider’s office. The clinic acknowledged a coding error and corrected it. My bill dropped to zero.

As an assistant professor of health policy and addiction studies at Penn State Harrisburg, I know whom to call and what questions to ask when I receive an unexpected medical bill. Many of my graduate students worked full time and took evening classes. Would they know how to dispute a bill, or have time?

Those experiences led me to investigate how often patients pay out of pocket for annual checkups. I teamed up with fellow researchers Erin Duffy and Max Crowley to examine this question. In our analysis of a Pennsylvania survey, nearly 1 in 4 insured respondents reported paying for their most recent checkup.
Why a preventive visit may come with a bill

Many health care services covered by insurance are subject to copayments or deductibles. A copayment is a fixed amount patients pay for a covered service, while a deductible is the amount they generally must pay for covered care before insurance starts paying.

The ACA, however, requires most health plans to cover certain recommended preventive services, including screenings for high blood pressure and certain cancers, vaccinations and counseling to help people quit smoking. These should come at no cost to patients.
Generally, this applies when patients see providers who are in their insurance plan’s network. But that doesn’t mean every annual checkup is free.

If a patient discusses a new symptom or asks the clinician to manage an existing condition during their annual checkup, it can result in a separate office-visit charge. A test may be billed as diagnostic rather than preventive, and coverage varies by plan and provider. Sometimes, as in my case, a coding error is responsible.
Not every charge is inappropriate. The challenge is that patients often cannot tell which services should be covered, why they were billed, or whether a mistake occurred.

Previous studies have found, using insurance claims, that patients sometimes face out-of-pocket costs during preventive visits. But these records show how visits were billed, not necessarily what patients believed they were receiving. We wanted to know whether people who thought they were getting annual checkups also reported paying out of pocket.

Our study, published in August 2026 in the peer-reviewed journal Prevention Science, used the 2024 Penn State Lion Poll, an online survey of Pennsylvania adults. We analyzed responses from 912 insured adults who reported an annual checkup within the preceding 10 years. Most had one in the past year.
Of those respondents, 23.5% reported paying out of pocket for their most recent checkup. Among those who paid, the average reported out-of-pocket amount was $68.50.

After accounting for other characteristics such as age, gender, insurance type, income and education, we found that respondents who were not familiar with ACA preventive-care protections were about 12 percentage points more likely to report paying than those who were familiar with the protections. That difference is equivalent to roughly 12 more people paying out of every 100.
Those who considered healthcare unaffordable were about 13 percentage points more likely to pay than those who found it affordable.

Because our survey relied on patients’ reports rather than billing records, we could not determine why individual charges occurred, or whether they were appropriate. The findings show associations, not causation, and our nonrandom sample cannot provide a precise statewide estimate.

I kept thinking about the student who said he would never return for another checkup. Research has shown that even modest out-of-pocket costs can discourage people from getting recommended screenings. Delaying preventive care could mean missing opportunities to detect health problems early, when treatment may be more effective.

Our survey did not find a statistically significant association between paying for a previous checkup and planning another one. However, respondents who were unfamiliar with ACA protections or considered healthcare unaffordable were less likely to plan a checkup. These findings suggest that uncertainty about costs may discourage people from seeking preventive care.

Before a visit, ask your insurer which preventive services are covered without cost-sharing and confirm that your provider is in-network. Ask the clinic whether discussing other health concerns or receiving additional tests could trigger a charge.

If a bill arrives, compare it with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, which you can typically find in your online insurance account or receive by mail. Ask the provider’s billing office which services and codes were submitted and request a correction if something appears wrong. You can also contact your insurer to question or appeal a coverage decision.
A colleague told me she challenged a $20 or $30 copayment requested at check-in for an annual visit after remembering our conversations. The charge was removed.

Patients should not have to become experts in insurance billing to receive preventive care. Clearer coverage information and more transparent billing could help people seek care without fearing unexpected costs.

articles.title: Some states are stepping up after federal childcare cuts – and now offer lessons for the future
articles.author: Caitlyn Collins, Associate Professor of Sociology, Washington University in St. Louis
paras: While affordability pressures are hitting Americans in many facets of their lives, from groceries to gas prices to housing costs, one important expense often gets less attention – childcare.

After a huge infusion of federal funds into childcare dried up at the end of the Biden administration, experts warned that this sharp cutoff, sometimes dubbed the “childcare cliff,” would force parents to either scale back work to handle the extra caretaking or pay steep costs out of pocket.

The potential effects of the federal cuts are hard to estimate, in part because states took different approaches in the aftermath. In some cases, they offset the sharp cuts in part by redirecting other funds to childcare.

But several states, including Vermont, New Mexico and Kentucky, have gone further and innovated on their own to shore up support for working parents and their young children. Meanwhile, New York City is expanding free toddler slots for lower-income families, following Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s announcement to build a universal early childcare system.

Taken together, these experiments point to bipartisan ways to support working parents, especially if the results of the November 2026 midterms signal a new willingness to tackle one of the biggest cost burdens for families.

As researchers of sociology and childcare policy with six children from 1 to 16 years old between us, we have also gained insights from our own data gathered over 75 interviews with parents in St. Louis, Missouri, over the past few years. We see them struggling with a fragmented childcare system that’s in need of a deep strategic investment. These families face limited choices and soaring costs for an essential good that allows a parent to go to work.

Out-of-pocket expenses for parents using center-based care in childcare centers and private preschool programs have more than doubled since 2019. In 2024, the national average price of childcare was US$13,128 annually, which rivals housing as the most expensive item in family budgets.

The disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic laid bare the critical role that reliable, high-quality childcare plays for working families. But we believe it also presented an opportunity for innovative investments in the nation’s fractured childcare landscape.

Pandemic relief legislation in 2021 directed nearly $40 billion to shore up the supply and quality of childcare. This funding increase, which was a fourfold jump over previous levels, supported childcare staff with higher wages and allowed for other investments to improve the quality of care.
The reach was vast, with stabilization funds flowing to 220,000 providers serving 9.6 million children. Many states also provided grants to create new slots and improve how providers got paid.

As those funds began drying up in September 2023, some states started to address these shortfalls on their own. In some cases, they took significant steps at a policy level to channel more support to working parents. We believe these investments could serve as examples for the rest of the country.

One is Vermont, which in 2023 became the first state to pass a law establishing a childcare entitlement. Following more than a decade of advocacy and bipartisan support, the law established a near-universal public childcare system, funded partially through a payroll tax of 0.44% split between employers and employees.

Through an expansion of subsidies along income tiers, the number of families covered rose by 55% from July 2022 to May 2025, while flexible grants increased the number of providers and focused on improving the quality of care. About 12,000 children are now covered under this program.

New Mexico went even further. In November 2025, the state became the first in the nation to offer universal childcare. Based on an older program that provided free childcare to low-income families, the initiative expanded support to all working parents regardless of income.
Before the expansion, 32,000 children were covered, a number the state aims to double by 2028. On average, the state estimates that the program will save families $12,000 a year.

Meanwhile, the Kentucky legislature in April 2026 passed a measure with strong bipartisan support to make major investments in the state’s childcare infrastructure. Key provisions include free childcare for the children of childcare center employees, increased state-subsidized reimbursement rates, and required training to support very young special needs children.

The Kentucky measure also loosened regulations that had made it tough for employers to share costs for care, such as renting facilities, while pitching a pilot program to open one-room “microcenters” in communities that lacked sufficient childcare options. In addition, Gov. Andy Beshear launched a complementary Pre-K for All pilot program in several counties.

Another example is New York City, where Mamdani has announced an expansion for toddlers as young as 2 years old in all five of the city’s boroughs, building on the city’s programs for free childcare for 3-K and pre-K. To date, this effort has increased some slots, although the rollout in September hit bumps.
The childcare crunch by the numbers

Given the skyrocketing costs, over 70% of families who sought care say it’s difficult to find childcare – and that doesn’t count the 11% who fail to find any at all, according to a 2023 government survey. That report found that families with Black or Hispanic children or infants, and those living in the South and West, are more likely to run into cost as a barrier.

On the supply side, three-quarters of providers say they have to turn many families away or put them on waiting lists. Center-based care for an infant costs more than in-state college tuition at a public university in 32 states, yet childcare workers, who are overwhelmingly women of color, earn the same as parking lot attendants and dog walkers. That makes them some of the lowest-paid workers in the entire economy.

Amid soaring costs and scarce supply, roughly half of all U.S. families live in so-called childcare deserts – areas where there are three children under 5 for every licensed-care slot. The answer for many families in these cases is to rely on ad hoc and irregular informal care. Some parents told us they’re turning to relatives and neighbors for help. Others resorted to using unlicensed, and potentially unsafe, childcare providers because they found no other viable options. And for some remote workers, the daunting solution is to care for their kids themselves while working.

The problem with such makeshift arrangements is that they tend, on average, to offer fewer of the learning opportunities linked to children’s long-term development and social mobility. And even these arrangements can be tough to afford: One single mother we interviewed told us she paid for a week’s childcare in kind with her own breast milk, which went to feed the care provider’s grandchildren. We also spoke to parents who reported choosing between childcare bills and heat, electricity or rent.

Another mom told us about a more unconventional solution. She and her husband work full time but can’t afford the childcare options in their community, so she decided to join a gym that provides free childcare while its members exercise. She brings her laptop and works, rather than working out, while her toddler plays.

These parents are scraping by in the absence of the affordable, subsidized childcare options commonplace in other countries. But this crunch is also a lose-lose proposition for the economy. The U.S. could lose as much as $290 billion per year by 2030 in forgone economic activity due to women not working or not working as much due to childcare pressures, according to the consultancy BCG.

The Trump administration has laid out its own vision. Vice President JD Vance announced in September 2026 a preliminary proposal to repurpose existing funds for childcare subsidies as a cash transfer to married parents, provided that one spouse stays home. We believe, however, this approach fails to reflect the real needs of the millions of U.S. parents who can’t pay their bills if they only get one paycheck. In fact, under the subsidy program that Vance cited, only 16% of eligible children are reached today anyway.
We believe, based on our research, that any comprehensive overhaul has four important components.

First is a robust national policy for paid family leave, which would let families make the best care decisions for newborns, infants and parents themselves rather than sprinting back to work. Paid family leave would also ease demand for scarce infant care in the market.

Second is an expansion of early childhood care and education programs. By publicly subsidizing childcare, particularly for low-income families and special needs kids, policymakers can help close the affordability gap for high-quality care.

Third is a greater investment in childcare workers. Qualified caregivers are the cornerstone of high-quality childcare. If their wages and working conditions improve, it means fewer will have to take side hustles or quit for better jobs.

Finally, providers will need more incentives to open in underserved areas. Childcare is expensive to provide and runs on thin margins. In low-income and rural areas, many families can’t pay prices that cover the true cost of care, and subsidy payments are often set below that cost. So opening a center there doesn’t make much financial sense. Startup grants, higher subsidy rates and operating support help close that gap, which makes it possible to open and stay open where need is greatest.

Caitlyn Collins receives funding from Pivotal, Arnold Ventures, and the Weidenbaum Center on the Economy, Government, and Public Policy at Washington University in St. Louis. She is affiliated with the American Sociological Association, Work and Family Researchers Network, and Council on Contemporary Families.

articles.title: Plans with cheaper premiums are risky business for Americans seeking lower healthcare costs
articles.author: Thomas Buchmueller, Professor of Business Economics and Public Policy, University of Michigan
paras: Healthcare costs are a major concern for Americans, and health insurance premiums are a primary fuel for that anxiety.

Shrinking federal subsidies for Affordable Care Act plans led to large premium increases for millions of Americans in 2025, causing many people to drop coverage. With premiums expected to rise further and Medicaid work requirements set to begin in January 2027, many Americans are left scrambling for affordable options.

We are health economists who study public policies aimed at expanding health insurance coverage. When it comes to our own health insurance, we are fortunate: We are among the roughly 160 million Americans who receive coverage through their employers.
But if you don’t work for a large employer that provides health benefits, finding coverage for your family can be confusing and, increasingly, expensive.
People looking for low-cost alternatives have no doubt encountered several options. They may look appealing and, in some cases, may be appropriate, but they can also carry real risks.

Historically, people who didn’t have access to employer-sponsored coverage had limited health insurance options. Before the Affordable Care Act went into effect in 2014, insurers could charge you a higher premium based on your health status, exclude coverage for preexisting medical conditions, or deny you coverage altogether.

The ACA eliminated this kind of discrimination, established a minimum standard of 10 essential benefits that health insurance plans had to cover, and required plans to fully cover the cost of preventive care. It also introduced income-based subsidies that could be used to purchase coverage in newly established online marketplaces.
Low-cost plans that aren’t available through ACA marketplaces are essentially vestiges of the pre-ACA health insurance landscape.

Regardless of where you get coverage, choosing health insurance involves trade-offs. The more you pay in premiums, the more comprehensive your coverage will be in terms of how much you must pay when you need care and the breadth of the network of covered providers.
Some trade-offs are clear when you choose a plan, but some lower-cost options may have limitations that are not immediately obvious.
Less costly short-term plans

As their name suggests, short-term, limited-duration plans are designed for people with temporary gaps in coverage, such as those who are between jobs or months away from qualifying for Medicare. These plans, which can be purchased for periods of up to six months, tend to be cheaper than marketplace coverage for two reasons.

First, because they are not subject to ACA rules, they may not provide the full range of essential health benefits. Short-term, limited-duration plans often do not cover maternity care and commonly don’t have an annual limit on out-of-pocket costs. In fact, these plans may cap how much they will pay in a year, leaving policyholders stuck with large, unexpected expenses.

Second, unlike plans offered through the ACA marketplaces, short-term, limited-duration plans are allowed to deny coverage based on your health status. Screening out higher-cost consumers reduces premiums, but if you are not in perfect health, you may not be able to find an insurer that will sell you one of these more limited plans.
Because of a concern that they destabilize the market by siphoning off healthy consumers, short-term, limited-duration plans are banned in five states.
Alternatives that look like insurance

Another seemingly affordable option is healthcare sharing ministries, arrangements through which consumers with common religious beliefs agree to share medical expenses. Their websites resemble those of health insurance companies – for example, they often present different plan options offering different levels of benefits – but they avoid using standard insurance terms like “premium” or “deductible” because these offerings are not insurance.

Because they are not regulated as insurance companies, healthcare sharing ministries are not subject to consumer protections or other state or federal requirements. There is also no guarantee that the ministry will cover your medical expenses when you submit a claim.

Like short-term, limited-duration plans, healthcare sharing ministries may deny coverage based on your health history, exclude coverage for preexisting conditions and put a limit on the dollar amount they will pay in benefits.

Another lower-cost option available in 14 states is health coverage offered by a farm bureau. These plans are similar to healthcare sharing ministries in that they are limited to a certain group of people – to enroll, you must be a member of the state’s farm bureau, though that does not mean you necessarily have to work in agriculture.

These plans are also not subject to federal or state insurance regulations. This means that, like short-term, limited-duration plans, they can offer lower prices by not offering certain benefits required by the ACA and by screening out high-cost consumers. Unlike short-term, limited-duration plans, there is no limit on how long you can hold farm bureau coverage.
Although the cost of marketplace coverage has increased dramatically since 2025, for many consumers who need coverage for more than six months, it remains the best option.

If you are single with an annual income below US$64,000, a couple with an annual income below $87,000, or a family of four with an annual income less than $132,000, you should still be eligible for a premium subsidy. And you will know that the plan you are purchasing is real insurance that covers a standard set of benefits and is subject to robust consumer protections.
If you are considering an alternative to marketplace coverage, there are a few things you should do to protect yourself:

Make sure you ask for a summary of benefits and coverage. This is a plain language summary of a health plan’s benefits and coverage with examples of how much the plan would cover for two specific conditions – diabetes and childbirth. Insurers and employers who offer coverage are required to provide this document to anyone applying for coverage. If they cannot provide one, what they are selling may not actually be insurance.

If they do provide a summary of benefits and coverage, read it carefully. As we noted earlier, one reason some options might be less expensive than a marketplace plan is that they provide much less coverage. Don’t assume that they cover all the benefits you would expect from a health insurance plan, or that they will cover the full cost of the care you receive.

Finally, never enter your phone number into a “do you need insurance” website. This area is rife with fraud, including multiple cases in which telemarketers misled consumers into paying hundreds of dollars per month to purchase sham health insurance.

Health insurance is expensive because healthcare is expensive – which means that consumers have to make difficult trade-offs. There is no easy answer, but beware of options that look too good to be true. They very well might be.

Thomas Buchmueller is a Non-Resident Senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution. He was part of a team that received state funding from 2015 to 2022 to evaluate the Healthy Michigan Plan, Michigan's ACA Medicaid expansion. In 2011-2012 he was the Senior Health Economist at the White House Council of Economic Advisers and from 2023-2025 he was Deputy Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

Helen Levy was part of a team that received state funding from 2015 to 2022 to evaluate the Healthy Michigan Plan, Michigan's ACA Medicaid expansion. She served as a Senior Economist at the White House Council of Economic Advisers in 2010-2011.

articles.title: New restrictions on purchases with SNAP benefits in some states mean fewer convenience stores are accepting them
articles.author: Benjamin Chrisinger, Assistant Professor of Community Health, Tufts University
paras: After 10 states began to add new restrictions to what people could buy with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits in early 2026, the number of convenience stores authorized to accept those benefits was 1.4% lower than would be expected based on trends in states without the policy change.
That’s what we found in our study, published in October 2026 in Health Affairs Scholar – a peer-reviewed journal.

SNAP, a federally funded program administered by the states, helps about 36 million low-income Americans afford groceries with government benefits that can be used at more than 250,000 stores to buy fresh fruit, ground beef, canned beans and other groceries. Using the benefits for many items, including hot food, alcohol, toiletries and pet food, has long been prohibited.

States can now obtain federal waivers to prohibit SNAP benefits from being used to buy other products. The 10 states with waivers that we studied had a mix of rules. Some only barred the sale of soda and other sugary drinks. Other prohibitions applied to energy drinks, candy, cake and other prepared desserts.

In states like Oklahoma and Florida that have adopted these new SNAP restrictions to discourage unhealthy diets, the number of convenience stores participating in the program has fallen relative to other states that haven’t made these changes. That was especially notable in areas with high numbers of low-income people where a large share of the population gets SNAP benefits.

We analyzed the number of stores participating in SNAP from January 2025 through June 2026 for the 10 states. We compared changes to that number before and after the waivers took effect with what happened in the rest of the country.

We found no clear evidence that the number of supermarkets or superstores was declining in waiver states. Although it’s slightly lower than otherwise expected, this effect is not statistically significant.

Because the restrictions vary, we also investigated whether the type mattered: sugary drinks only, or sugary drinks plus other products that state officials wanted to discourage. We found the largest declines in the number of SNAP-authorized convenience stores in states restricting both drinks and candy: an average of 2.2%.

Stores in waiver states may need to update their checkout systems and train employees to prevent purchases that are no longer allowed with SNAP benefits – potentially a time-consuming burden for some retailers. That may help explain why the number of SNAP-authorized convenience stores is declining.
Although most people use SNAP benefits to buy food at big stores, they also purchase some groceries at convenience stores, especially in neighborhoods where there are few supermarkets.

Other federal policies are also changing how SNAP works due to provisions in the big tax and policy legislation that Congress passed in July 2025. It changed some eligibility rules and how much states pay to administer the program.

Even before all those changes take effect, many people who are likely eligible for SNAP benefits are having a harder time getting them, due to the steps states are taking to prepare for the new rules. The number of Americans enrolled in the program is falling fast despite no sign that their needs are shrinking.
We focused on changes to the number of stores authorized to accept SNAP in states with waivers. We didn’t study whether stores closed, or exactly why stores left the program.

We also don’t know what role court rulings will play. On June 22, near the end of our study, a federal court invalidated SNAP food restrictions in five states: Colorado, Iowa, Nebraska, Tennessee and West Virginia. Waiver programs in other states – Indiana, Utah, Idaho, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Texas and Florida – were allowed to continue.
Four states had similar restrictions in the works: South Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio and Virginia. Those plans are on hold.

Beginning in November 2026, most U.S. stores will also have to meet new requirements of a different kind to participate in SNAP. They’ll need to stock a wider variety of staple foods, such as grains, dairy products and produce. These requirements could pose additional challenges for convenience stores.
Further research is needed to see if the effects we found change over time, including in states that introduce these restrictions after the period we studied.
